overview: Akan describes several related peoples, including the Asante and Fante, rather than one kingdom. Their histories include distinctive local institutions and connections with neighbors. Weaving shows how shared skills and changing fashions can cross political and linguistic boundaries without making every community identical.

periods.title: Begho in the regional trading network
periods.summary: An early archaeological report placed Begho’s main settlement around 1350 to 1725. The town provides regional evidence for exchange and craft production. These approximate site dates neither define all Akan settlement nor verify the map’s changing boundaries.

periods.title: Changing markets for woven cloth
periods.summary: From the 1950s, growing demand encouraged both Asante and Ewe weavers to develop colorful rayon cloths. Kraamer’s fieldwork traced exchange and innovation across weaving centres, alongside competing accounts of where kente originated.

items.text: Begho included quarters associated with local Brong communities and others occupied by Mande-speaking Muslims. Posnansky’s account of the 1970s excavations reports spindle whorls and dye pits, concrete evidence for textile work. The town’s mixed population cautions against assigning every recovered technology to one ethnic group.

Brassworking took place in Begho’s Dwinfuor artisans’ quarter, while iron was smelted outside the town at Dapaa. Weights made from stone and terracotta also survived. These different materials connect specialist production with measurement and exchange; they do not mean every household performed the same work or possessed equal wealth.

The excavations also uncovered decorated ivory trumpets and a shrine room containing inverted offering cups. Posnansky interpreted these as evidence for the ritual character of Brong chieftaincy. The objects and their arrangement are observations; the explanation of their political and religious role is an interpretation informed by local historical research.

The Met’s brass shell-form object, catalogue 1978.412.450, is dated broadly from the nineteenth to mid-twentieth century. The catalogue explains lost-wax casting: a model is enclosed in clay, removed by heating, and replaced by molten metal. This is a museum object with a broad regional attribution, not a find from Begho.

Gold-dust exchange required scales, containers, spoons and carefully adjusted weights. The Met’s recent discussion distinguishes geometric weights from figurines often grouped under the same name. Some figurines may instead have circulated as embodiments of proverbs or moral ideas. A familiar museum label therefore does not establish every object’s original function.

Kente cloth is assembled by sewing narrow woven strips edge to edge. Asante and Ewe centres developed related but distinguishable repertoires, and later exchanged styles and materials. Kraamer’s research traces these interactions and competing origin stories; it does not support reducing the whole tradition to one securely dated invention by a single people.

sections.title: Household tools, food and living heritage

items.text: In Mpraeso, Kwahu women potters shape clay into coils and build vessels on a raised working surface. A study published in 2020 records a wooden paddle, sabroba, used to flatten bases and a metal scraper, ponoye, used inside pots. The named tools show how control of shape and surface depends on practiced handwork.

The potters pack vessels on firewood for open firing in their backyards. Some fired pots are placed in sawdust to blacken them. The study follows production through sale, connecting material preparation and firing with a working household economy. These observations concern the surveyed Mpraeso potters, not an unchanged practice everywhere in Akan history.

Mpraeso grinding bowls, apotoyowa, have ridged interiors for preparing vegetables with wooden pestles. Other vessels store drinking water, cook food or serve meals. Their shapes meet different household tasks, so pottery history includes ordinary food preparation and water storage as well as objects used in ceremonies.

Asante shrine compounds near Kumasi use timber and bamboo frames with mud plaster, organized around courtyards. Reliefs on the walls carry animal, plant and geometric forms associated with meanings and beliefs. These surviving buildings document one Akan architectural tradition; they should not be treated as a standard house type for every Akan community.

Many of the protected shrine buildings have been reconstructed or modified, including replacements of thatched roofs and earthen floors. Conservation involves chiefs, Elders, residents and museum staff. Their survival reflects continued decisions about use and repair, rather than the preservation of buildings entirely untouched since the Asante kingdom’s height.

ending.text: Akan peoples do not share a single fall date: individual kingdoms and political institutions have separate histories. Living shrine traditions and community participation in their preservation demonstrate continuity. The end of the map’s Akan interval in 1715 must not be read as the disappearance of these communities.
